4× [[Southeastern Conference football individual awards#Coach of the Year|SEC Coach of the Year]] (1936, 1938, 1950, 1951) | coaching_records = | CFBHOF_year = 1956 | CFBHOF_id = 1583 }} '''Robert Reese Neyland''' ({{respell|KNEE|lənd}};{{Cite web |last=Painter |first=John |last2=Magill |first2=Matt |date=2012-03-28 |title=Neyland: 50 Facts on 50th Anniversary |url=https://utsports.com/news/2012/3/28/neyland_50_facts_on_50th_anniversary.aspx |access-date=2025-06-03 |website=University of Tennessee Athletics}}{{Cite web |date=February 3, 2008 |title="KNEE-land, LIKE MY KNEE" |url=http://blogs.knoxnews.com/mattingly/2008/02/kneeland-like-my-knee.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130611031848/http://blogs.knoxnews.com/mattingly/2008/02/kneeland-like-my-knee.html |archive-date=June 11, 2013 |access-date=December 16, 2011 |website=Knoxville News Sentinel}} February 17, 1892 – March 28, 1962) was an American [[American football|football]] player and coach and officer in the [[United States Army]], reaching the rank of [[Brigadier general (United States)|brigadier general]]. He served three stints as the head football coach at the [[University of Tennessee]] (UTK) from 1926 to 1934, 1936 to 1940, and 1946 to 1952. He is one of two college football coaches to have won national titles in two [[List of college football head coaches with non-consecutive tenure|non-consecutive tenures]] at the same school, along with [[Frank Leahy]] of the [[University of Notre Dame]]. Neyland holds the record for most wins in [[Tennessee Volunteers football|Tennessee Volunteers]] history with 173 wins in 216 games, six undefeated seasons, nine undefeated regular seasons, seven conference championships, and four claimed [[NCAA Division I FBS national football championship|national championships]]. At UTK, he reeled off undefeated streaks of 33, 28, 23, 19, and 14 games. Neyland is often referred to as one of the best, if not the best, defensive football coaches ever. ''[[Sports Illustrated]]'' named Neyland as the [[defensive coordinator]] of its all-century college football team in its "Best of the 20th Century" edition.{{cite magazine|url=http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/centurys_best/news/1999/10/06/cfb_allcentury_team/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20000824074230/http://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/centurys_best/news/1999/10/06/cfb_allcentury_team/ |archive-date=August 24, 2000 |title=CNN/SI - Century's Best - SI's NCAA Football All-Century Team - Wednesday October 06, 1999 03:30 PM |magazine=Sports Illustrated|date= October 6, 1999|access-date=December 28, 2009}} 112 of his victories came via shutout. In 1938 and 1939, Neyland's Vols set [[National Collegiate Athletic Association|NCAA]] records when they shut out 17 straight regular season opponents for 71 consecutive shutout quarters. His [[1939 Tennessee Volunteers football team|1939 squad]] is the last NCAA team in history to hold every regular season opponent scoreless.{{citation needed|date=September 2021}} Neyland was also an innovator. He is credited with being the first coach to utilize sideline telephones and game film to study opponents. His teams also were some of the first to wear lightweight pads and tearaway jerseys. Such measures increased his players' elusiveness and exemplify Neyland's "speed over strength" philosophy. Neyland is also famous for creating the seven "Game Maxims" of football that many coaches, on all levels, still use. Tennessee players recite the maxims before every game in the locker room as a team. [[Neyland Stadium]] at UTK is not only named for The General, but its present form was designed by him. The plans he drew up for a major expansion shortly before his death formed the basis for all expansions that brought the stadium to its modern size with an over 100,000 seat capacity. Neyland was inducted into the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] as a coach in 1956. On November 12, 2010, a {{convert|9|ft|m|adj=on}}, nearly {{convert|1,500|lb|adj=on}} bronze statue of General Neyland was unveiled between gates 15A and 17 at Neyland Stadium. The statue, which was commissioned by artist Blair Buswell, is twice life-size. Since Neyland is portrayed in the kneeling position rather than standing, the statue is {{convert|9|ft}} tall (a standing statue would have stood {{convert|12|ft}} tall). The base is {{convert|57|by|87|in|cm}} and features Neyland's well-known seven Game Maxims engraved into the precast. ==Early life, playing career, and education== [[File:Robert Reese Neyland Jr. (1892–1962) at West Point in 1916.png|thumb|right|150px|At West Point in 1916]] Born in [[Greenville, Texas]], Neyland attended Burleson Junior College in his home town for a year.{{Cite web |last=Dempsey |first=John Mark |date=September 8, 2015 |title=Gen. Robert Neyland: Hunt County's most accomplished person? |url=https://www.ketr.org/news/2015-09-08/gen-robert-neyland-hunt-countys-most-accomplished-person |access-date=March 17, 2024 |website=88.9 KETR |language=en}} He transferred to [[Texas A&M University]] for a year before receiving an appointment to the [[United States Military Academy]] at [[West Point, New York]] from Congressman [[Sam Rayburn]]. At West Point, Neyland starred as a lineman in football and a [[pitcher]] in [[baseball]], throwing the program's first [[no-hitter]] and was the academy [[boxing]] champion three consecutive years.{{Cite web |title=Robert Reese Neyland Jr. (2004) - Hall of Fame |url=https://goarmywestpoint.com/honors/hall-of-fame/robert-reese-neyland-jr-/17 |access-date=2024-08-24 |website=Army West Point |language=en}} The [[National League (baseball)|National League]] baseball [[New York Giants (NL)|New York Giants]] offered him a $3,500 contract (equivalent to $100,000 in 2024), which he turned down.{{Cite web |title=Bob Neyland (1956) - Hall of Fame |url=https://footballfoundation.org/hof.aspx?hof=1583 |access-date=March 17, 2024 |website=[[National Football Foundation]] |language=en}} Neyland graduated, 28th in a class of 125, from West Point in June 1916. He was commissioned as an officer in the [[United States Army Corps of Engineers]] and served in France during [[World War I]]. After the war, he attended [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT) for a graduate degree in engineering before returning to West Point as [[aide-de-camp]] to Superintendent [[Douglas MacArthur]].{{Cite web |last=Vergun |first=David |date=November 17, 2020 |title=Sports Heroes Who Served: Tennessee Football Coach Served in World Wars I, II |url=https://www.defense.gov/News/Feature-Stories/story/Article/2411661/sports-heroes-who-served-tennessee-football-coach-served-in-world-wars-i-ii/https://www.defense.gov/News/Feature-Stories/Story/Article/2411661/sports-heroes-who-served-tennessee-football-coach-served-in-world-wars-i-ii/ |access-date=March 17, 2024 |website=U.S. Department of Defense |language=en-US}}{{dead link|date=December 2025|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}} ==Coaching career== {{More citations needed section|date=October 2020}} [[File:NeylandStatue.jpg|thumb|left|Statue of Robert Neyland on display at [[Neyland Stadium]]]] Wanting to continue coaching, Captain Neyland was appointed Professor of Military Science at the [[University of Tennessee]] (UTK) in 1925.{{Cite web |title=Collection: General Robert Neyland Papers |url=https://scout.lib.utk.edu/repositories/2/resources/731 |access-date=March 17, 2024 |website=SCOUT}} After one season as an assistant to head coach [[M. B. Banks]], Neyland was named head coach and [[athletic director]] by chairman of the UTK Athletic Council [[Nathan Dougherty|Nathan W. Dougherty]] in 1926. He coached the team for nine years before the Army called him to active duty for one year in [[Panama]]. During that first nine-year stint with the Vols, Neyland had five undefeated seasons, all within a six-year period (1927, 1928, 1929, 1931, and 1932). The Vols reeled off undefeated streaks of 33 and 28 straight games.{{Cite web |last=Lay |first=Ken |date=October 14, 2023 |title=A look at Robert Neyland's ties to Tennessee, Texas A&M |url=https://volswire.usatoday.com/2023/10/14/a-look-at-robert-neylands-ties-to-tennessee-texas-am/ |access-date=March 18, 2024 |website=Vols Wire|publisher=USA Today |language=en-US}} Upon returning stateside from the [[Panama Canal Zone]], he returned to UTK as head coach. Neyland's 1938 team went undefeated and was proclaimed national champion by several minor outlets.{{Cite web |title=1938 Tennessee Volunteers Schedule and Results |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/tennessee/1938-schedule.html |access-date=March 18, 2024 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en}}{{Cite web |date=June 14, 2017 |title=National Championships |url=https://utsports.com/sports/2017/6/14/history-ncaa-html.aspx |access-date=March 18, 2024 |website=University of Tennessee Athletics |language=en}} His 1939 squad is notable for being the last college football team to go an entire regular season unscored upon, shutting out every opponent; his team was then shut out by USC in the Rose Bowl.{{Cite web |title=1939 Tennessee Volunteers Schedule and Results |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/tennessee/1939-schedule.html |access-date=March 18, 2024 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en}} From November 5, 1938, to December 9, 1939, the Vols ran off 17 straight shutouts and 71 consecutive shutout quarters—records that have never been seriously threatened.{{Cite web |title=Robert Neyland "The General" |url=https://timeline.utk.edu/history/head-coach-neyland |access-date=March 17, 2024 |website=UTK.edu}} Neyland completed another undefeated regular season in 1940 before falling in the Sugar Bowl to Boston College.{{Cite web |title=1940 Tennessee Volunteers Schedule and Results |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/tennessee/1940-schedule.html |access-date=March 17, 2024 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en}} He was recalled to military service again in 1941.{{Cite web |last=Vergun |first=David |date=January 12, 2024 |title=Tennessee Volunteers Football Coach Robert Neyland Served in Both World Wars |url=https://www.military.com/veteran-jobs/tennessee-volunteers-football-coach-robert-neyland-served-both-world-wars.html |access-date=March 18, 2024 |website=Military.com |language=en}} In fall 1942, Neyland was appointed as head coach of an [[List of World War II military service football teams|Eastern All-Army]] team that took on [[National Football League]] clubs to raise money for the [[Army Emergency Relief]] fund.{{cite news|last=Turkin|first=Hy|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/32136662/army_gridders_aim_at_million_goal/|title=Army Gridders Aim At Million $ Goal|newspaper=[[New York Daily News]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=July 16, 1942|access-date=June 4, 2019}} The Eastern All-Army played three games, defeating the [[1942 New York Giants season|New York Giants]] and [[Brooklyn Dodgers (NFL)|Brooklyn Dodgers]],{{cite news|last=Fraley|first=Oscar|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/32167809/|title=Pingel, Cafego Stanlee Pace Soldier Team|agency=[[United Press|UP]]|newspaper=The Scrantonian|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=September 13, 1942|access-date=June 4, 2019}}{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/32217250/|title=All-Army Football Team Rallies To Nip Brooklyn Dodgers, 13-7|agency=[[United Press|UP]]|newspaper=[[Herald News]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=September 17, 1942|access-date=June 4, 2019}} but lost to the defending NFL champion [[1942 Chicago Bears season|Chicago Bears]].{{cite news|last=King|first=Bill|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/32220677/|title=Army Grid All-Stars Disband After Giving Bears Great Fight|agency=[[Associated Press|AP]]|newspaper=[[The News Journal]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=September 21, 1942|access-date=June 4, 2019}} Along with the Western All-Army team led by [[Duke University]]'s [[Wallace Wade]], the games raised $241,392.29 for the fund.{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/32234903/army_gets_grid_check/|title=Army Gets Grid Check|agency=[[Associated Press|AP]]|newspaper=[[Arizona Republic]]|via=[[Newspapers.com]]|date=November 8, 1942|access-date=June 4, 2019}} In [[World War II]], Neyland served in the [[China-Burma-India Theater]], supervising the transportation of materiel through [[monsoons]] and across the [[Himalayas]] to the troops commanded by [[general officer|General]] "Vinegar" [[Joe Stillwell]]. During his military career he was awarded the [[Distinguished Service Medal (U.S. Army)|Distinguished Service Medal]] and the [[Legion of Merit]] and made a member of the [[Order of the British Empire]].{{Cite web |last=Hickman |first=Herman |date=October 25, 1954 |title=NEYLAND'S BOYS |url=https://vault.si.com/vault/1954/10/25/neylands-boys |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201128023829/https://vault.si.com/vault/1954/10/25/neylands-boys |archive-date=November 28, 2020 |access-date=March 17, 2024 |website=Sports Illustrated Vault |language=en-us}} He retired from military service a second time, in 1946, with the rank of brigadier general, and again returned to the Vols as coach through 1952. After producing mediocre teams in the late forties, many thought that the General had lost his touch, as more teams moved toward the "T formation" and Neyland continued running the single wing. Neyland was vindicated, however, as he ended his career with a flourish. His 1950 team was crowned national champion by several minor outlets, while his 1951 team won the school's first undisputed national championship, the first year the Volunteers ended a season ranked first in either the [[Associated Press|AP]] or [[United Press International|UPI]] poll.{{Cite web |title=1951 Tennessee Volunteers Schedule and Results |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/tennessee/1951-schedule.html |access-date=March 18, 2024 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en}}{{Cite web |title=1951 College Football Polls |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/years/1951-polls.html |access-date=March 18, 2024 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en}} He coached his final season in 1952, leading the Vols to a 8–2–1 record.{{Cite web |title=1952 Tennessee Volunteers Schedule and Results |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/tennessee/1952-schedule.html |access-date=March 18, 2024 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en}} He remained as athletic director at the university until his death in [[New Orleans]] on March 28, 1962.{{Cite web |date=March 29, 1962 |title=Gen. Robert Neyland, 70, Dead; Coached Football at Tennessee; Led Teams to 171 Victories in 27 Years N.C.A.A. Aide Was in Hall of Fame |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1962/03/29/archives/gen-robert-neyland-70-dead-coached-football-at-tennessee-led-teams.html |access-date=March 18, 2024 |website=The New York Times |language=en-US}} [[File:Robert Neyland (c. 1915).png|thumb|Neyland at Army tossing a pass]] Shortly before his death, Neyland drew up plans for a major expansion and renovation to the Vols' home stadium, Shields–Watkins Field. When he had arrived in Knoxville in 1925, Shields–Watkins Field seated only 3,200 people—barely a fraction of the capacity of [[Vanderbilt Commodores football|Vanderbilt]]'s [[Dudley Field]]. Reflecting the Vols' rise to national prominence under his watch, the stadium's capacity had jumped to over 46,000 seats—an over 14-fold increase—in the 36 years since then. UT renamed the stadium [[Neyland Stadium]] in his honor prior to the 1962 season, and the plans he drew up were so far ahead of their time that they have been used as the basis for every major expansion since then.{{Cite web |last=Ramey |first=Grant |date=July 29, 2020 |title=Tracing Neyland Stadium's history, from 1921 to 2020 |url=https://247sports.com/college/tennessee/longformarticle/tennessee-vols-football-tracing-neyland-stadiums-history-from-1921-to-2020-149629256/ |access-date=March 17, 2024 |website=247Sports |language=en}} ==Family== {{Unreferenced section|date=October 2020}} [[File:Gen._Robert_R._Neyland_tombstone.jpg|200px|thumb|right|Tombstone of General Neyland at [[Knoxville National Cemetery]]]] On July 16, 1923, Neyland married Ada "Peggy" Fitch (September 1, 1897 – March 7, 1976) of [[Grand Rapids, Michigan]]. They had met while she was visiting friends at the academy. Ada was the daughter of Charles Lewis Fitch (July 24, 1845 – September 8, 1930) and Mary S. (June 1853 – ?). They had two sons, Robert Jr., born February 11, 1930, and Lewis, December 6, 1933 — 2013. General Neyland was the son of lawyer Robert Reece Neyland Sr. (October 1859 – 1935) and Pauline Lewis Neyland (January 1861 – December 1932). His siblings were sister Carroll M. Neyland (January 1890 – 1965) and brother Mayo W. Neyland (March 1896 – November 1969). Both General Neyland and Ada are buried in [[Knoxville National Cemetery]]. ==Neyland Scholarship== {{Unreferenced section|date=October 2020}} In late 1961, Neyland began working on a plan for supporters of UT athletic teams to show their interest in UT's academic programs by offering scholarships to attract outstanding student scholars to the university. General Neyland himself was an outstanding scholar, as well as an athlete during his college days at West Point. It was the General's dream that the university offer four-year academic merit scholarships to students who possessed outstanding academic and leadership qualities. Following Neyland's death in early 1962, [[Andrew D. Holt|Dr. Andrew D. Holt]], then UT president, announced that a nationwide campaign would be launched to raise a minimum of $100,000 to establish the Robert R. Neyland Scholarship Fund. In October 1962, at half-time of the UT vs. [[University of Alabama|Alabama]] game, 165 women representing UT's [[sorority|sororities]] collected more than $10,000 in a 15-minute time period at Neyland Stadium to launch the effort. By the end of fall 1962, more than $65,000 had been committed to the Neyland Scholarship fund. In the spring of 1963, a decision was made that proceeds from the annual Orange and White spring football game would go to help build the Neyland Scholarship Fund. The first Neyland Scholarships were awarded in 1963.{{Cite web |last=Reynolds |first=Jason |date=April 23, 1997 |title=Neyland Scholars recognized |url=https://www.utdailybeacon.com/news/neyland-scholars-recognized/article_6744b30e-de04-591f-9546-f0021489ba3a.html |access-date=March 17, 2024 |website=The Daily Beacon |language=en}} The first two recipients were Melissa Ann Baker of [[Maryville, Tennessee]] (now Ann Baker Furrow, a former member of the UT Board of Trustees) and Robert English Allen of [[Columbia, Tennessee]]. ==Seven Maxims of Football== During the 1930s, Neyland began having his teams recite seven sentences that he felt summarized everything it took to win a game. These came to be known as "the Seven Maxims of Football", or "the Seven Game Maxims."{{Cite web |last=Pate |first=Josh |date=September 22, 2010 |title=Seven Pillars of Tennessee Football |url=https://utsports.com/news/2010/9/22/seven_pillars_of_tennessee_football.aspx |access-date=March 17, 2024 |website=University of Tennessee Athletics |language=en}} *The team that makes the fewest mistakes will win. *Play for and make the breaks and when one comes your way – SCORE. *If at first the game – or the breaks – go against you, don't let up... put on more steam. *Protect our kickers, our QB, our lead and our ball game. *Ball, [[Glossary of American football terms#oskie|oskie]], cover, block, cut and slice, pursue and gang tackle... for this is the WINNING EDGE. *Press the kicking game.
